title: Delimitation Debate Dominates as India's Parliament Opens Stormy Monsoon Session
excerpt: The Modi government has dropped the controversial Delimitation Bill from the formal agenda, but opposition parties plan to make it the session's central battleground alongside NEET leaks and Ram Temple donations.
body:
• India's Parliament begins its Monsoon Session on Monday with 19 sittings planned through August 13, amid street protests and opposition fury over multiple issues.
  • The government has not included the Delimitation Bill in the formal agenda of seven bills, despite earlier efforts to pass it in a special April session where it fell short of the required two-thirds majority.
  • The INDIA opposition bloc is coordinating a joint floor strategy around delimitation, NEET paper leaks, alleged Ram Temple donation misuse, and inflation.
  • The proposed delimitation would increase Lok Sabha seats from 550 to 850, a move southern states fear will dilute their representation for having successfully controlled population growth.

A Session Under Siege

India's Parliament opens its Monsoon Session on Monday against the backdrop of mass street protests, a hunger-striking activist forcibly hospitalized, and an opposition determined to turn every session into a confrontation. The four-week session — running through August 13 — may prove to be one of the most contentious in recent memory.

The government has announced a legislative agenda of seven bills, including five new ones: amendments to tighten birth and death registration, revise the Income Tax Act, amend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, update the MSME Development Act, and a Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill replacing an ordinance. The FCRA Amendment Bill, governing foreign contributions, is also listed for consideration.

The Delimitation Question

Conspicuously absent from the formal agenda is the Delimitation Bill — a package of two Constitutional Amendment Bills that would increase the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850 seats and redraw parliamentary constituency boundaries. The government attempted to pass these bills during a special Parliament session in April, arguing they were necessary to implement the Women's Reservation Act before the 2029 elections.

That attempt failed. Even with 528 of 543 Lok Sabha MPs present, the government fell short of the two-thirds supermajority required for a constitutional amendment. Sources told Madhyamam that the delimitation package could be reconsidered after fresh Union Cabinet approval.

"Even with 528 of 543 Lok Sabha MPs present, the government fell short of the two-thirds supermajority required for a constitutional amendment."

"Even with 528 of 543 Lok Sabha MPs present, the government fell short of the two-thirds supermajority required for a constitutional amendment."

The opposition united against the proposals in April on a fundamental argument: delimitation based primarily on population would benefit Hindi-speaking northern states — where the BJP is electorally dominant — while punishing southern states like Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka that successfully implemented family planning programs. Congress's K.C. Venugopal told The Hindu that delimitation "is not just an INDIA bloc issue" but "concerns our Constitutional framework."

"States that successfully controlled their population would lose representation while those that didn't would gain seats — this is the core inequity the opposition is fighting."

— Based on opposition arguments reported by Dainik Jagran

Opposition's Multi-Front Strategy

The INDIA opposition bloc, led by Congress, has reached out to alliance partners including the DMK, Aam Aadmi Party, and regional parties to build a coordinated floor strategy. According to Dainik Jagran, Congress plans to raise issues including examination paper leaks, inflation, unemployment, and what it describes as irregularities in political funding.

Three issues are expected to dominate opposition disruptions:

NEET paper leaks: The ongoing examination scandal has spawned a nationwide protest movement, with tens of thousands expected to march to Parliament on Monday. Opposition parties want to force a formal debate on the crisis and demand Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

Ram Temple donations: Multiple opposition parties, including the Shiv Sena (UBT) and Congress, want to discuss alleged misuse of donations collected for the Ayodhya Ram Temple. Shiv Sena-UBT leader Priyanka Chaturvedi has demanded the government respond, citing the "historical significance" of the temple movement.

Delimitation: Even without the bill on the formal agenda, opposition parties plan to keep the issue alive through debates and procedural motions. TMC's Derek O'Brien has written to Prime Minister Modi demanding an all-party meeting on delimitation and foreign contribution bills. The DMK is expected to reiterate that any delimitation exercise must not disadvantage states that effectively implemented family planning.

What the Diaspora Should Know

For overseas Indians, two aspects of this session matter directly. Delimitation could reshape India's political geography for decades — and with it, the development priorities of states where many NRIs have roots. Southern states fear that losing Lok Sabha seats means losing bargaining power for infrastructure spending, education funding, and investment incentives.

The FCRA Amendment Bill also warrants attention. Changes to foreign contribution regulations could affect how diaspora organizations, NGOs, and religious institutions channel funds into India. The bill seeks to ensure foreign inflows "do not affect national interest, public order or national security," but critics worry the broad language could be used to restrict legitimate diaspora philanthropy.

What's Next

The session opens Monday and runs through August 13. With street protests at the doorstep, an energized opposition, and constitutional questions about India's democratic structure, the next four weeks will test whether India's Parliament can function as a deliberative body — or devolve into the procedural warfare that has defined recent sessions.
